bibliography.abstract: Infrastructure-based radar systems offer robust and long-range solutions for traffic monitoring, yet their detection and tracking performance under real-world conditions remains insufficiently evaluated. This study introduces DRaT (Drone and Radar Trajectories), a dual-modality dataset of naturalistic vehicle trajectories collected at a highway merging segment in Fort Worth, Texas, to systematically assess radar sensing performance against drone-derived ground truth. The performance is evaluated at three levels: individual vehicle detection, trajectory tracking, and macroscopic traffic parameter estimation. For individual vehicle detection, the radar achieves an overall precision of 78% and a recall of 57%, with degraded performance under congested traffic conditions and at longer distances. At the trajectory level, the radar demonstrates reasonably strong tracking performance (IDF1 = 0.699), maintaining reliable vehicle identities when tracks are successfully established. For macroscopic traffic flow metrics, the radar accurately estimates space-mean speed (MAPE < 4%) but underestimates density and volume by approximately 23% due to missed detections. The paper also discusses practical deployment considerations and potential downstream applications of roadside radar sensing systems. To support reproducible research on infrastructure-based sensing systems, we have open-sourced the DRaT dataset on Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/20171110.
bibliography.comment: Accepted by IEEE ITSC 2026. Compared with the accepted version, this version includes an expanded trajectory tracking analysis with additional evaluation metrics
bibliography.title: A Systematic Evaluation of Infrastructure-Based Radar System for Highway Traffic Monitoring

en.caveats: The evaluation is based on a single highway merging segment, meaning the performance metrics may not generalize to more complex urban intersections or different geometric layouts.
en.what: This study evaluates infrastructure-based radar performance using DRaT, a new dual-modality dataset of vehicle trajectories collected at a highway merging segment in Fort Worth, Texas, validated against drone-derived ground truth. The radar achieved a 78% precision and 57% recall for individual vehicle detection, with performance dropping under congestion and at greater distances. While it tracked trajectories with an IDF1 score of 0.699 and estimated space-mean speed with a mean absolute percentage error under 4%, it underestimated traffic density and volume by roughly 23% due to missed detections.
en.why: It establishes the first systematic, multi-level benchmark for roadside radar systems against high-fidelity drone imagery, quantifying the exact margin of error practitioners must expect when using radar for macroscopic traffic flow estimation.
